newsitem.title: GERMANY: German FDP sees budget scope to buy Eurofighter.
newsitem.headline: German FDP sees budget scope to buy Eurofighter.

text.p: The Free Democrat party (FDP), the smallest partner in Germany's three-party governing alliance, said on Friday there was still scope in the 1997 budget to pay for production of the Eurofighter combat jet to start.

FDP budget spokesman Wolfgang Weng said he expected parliament's budget committee to tackle the issue in the first quarter of 1997 -- but the four countries behind the project would have to hold talks before a final decision was made.
Earlier this week coalition leaders agreed to delay a decision on placing a firm order for Germany's 180 Eurofighters until early next year.

The government has set aside 100 million marks ($66.4 million) in its budget to cover potential costs next year. Dasa, the German partner in the Eurofighter consortium, wants an initial payment of at least 392 million marks.

Britain and Spain have already said they would buy their Eurofighters, putting Germany under increasing pressure to make a commitment. Any delay, the aircraft's makers warn, could cause costs to explode.

Defence Minister Volker Ruehe has indicated he wants to buy Eurofighter, and if necessary cut other defence procurement. MeanwhileFinance Minister Theo Waigel -- mindful of jobs it would secure in his home state of Bavaria -- has also supported the project.

One way out of the financial squeeze for Germany could be to redirect subsidies from the Airbus consortium, of which Dasa is also part, once it reaches the profit zone after 2000, said Dietrich Austermann, who represents Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) on parliament's defence committee.
Dasa is seeking 6.9 billion marks in interim financing to cover the production phase up to the delivery of the first finished Eurofighter in 2001.

But Austermann, speaking to Die Welt newspaper, warned: "This money cannot be raised in the medium term from the budget." The funds could be raised only if Airbus subsidies due for repayment later were taken into account, he said.

Die Welt added that this model would enable Germany to reply positively to a recent letter from British Prime Minister John Major calling for Germany urgently to meet its contractual obligation to finance the production of the Eurofighter.
Dasa, a unit of Daimler-Benz AG, has a 30 percent stake in the Eurofighter consortium. British Aerospace (Bae) owns 37.5 percent, Italy's Alenia 19.5 percent and Spain's Casa 13 percent.
